entries.meaning: Having attempted his crooked stratagem, Indra worried that the success or failure of the whole enterprise now lay in Bharata's hands. Janaka approached Raghunātha, and all the lights of the Solar line honored him. Then, at a time and in an assembly not opposed to duty, the family priest of Raghu's house spoke. He recounted the exchange between Janaka and Bharata and repeated Bharata's lovely declaration: ‘Dear Rāma, whatever command you give, he will carry out; this too is my counsel.’ Hearing this, Raghunātha joined both hands and answered in truthful, simple, gentle speech: ‘When the lord of Mithilā is himself present, anything I say will be uncultivated in every way. Whatever your counsel and command may be, I swear by you that I shall rightly bear it upon my head.’ At Rāma's oath the sage and Janaka shrank with embarrassment along with the assembly. Everyone looked toward Bharata's face, but no answer would come.

Seeing the whole assembly constrained by reserve, Rāma's brother gathered deep courage. Noting the difficult moment, he mastered his affection, checking its swelling like Agastya restraining the Vindhya. Grief had carried away the earth of the golden-eyed Bharata's understanding, but the vast boar of discernment, born of the spotless virtues of the Source of the world, effortlessly raised it at that moment. Bharata bowed to all and joined his hands, appealing to Rāma, the king, the guru, and the saints: ‘Forgive what is exceedingly improper in me today: with a tender face I shall speak hard words. Remembering lovely Sarasvatī in his heart, he brought her from the Mānasa of his mind to the lotus of his mouth. Bharata's speech became a charming female swan furnished with stainless discernment, duty, and wise policy. With the assembly softened by affection yet watching through the eyes of discernment, Bharata bowed, remembered Sītā and Raghurāja, and spoke.

‘Lord, you are father, mother, friend, guru, master, supremely venerable, the highest benefactor, and the knower within. You are a gracious and guileless master, a treasury of character, protector of those who bow, all-knowing, and wise. You are capable, benevolent to those who seek refuge, a connoisseur of virtue, and remover of faults and sins. No master is equal to my Lord, and there is no servant equal to me—I invoke you as witness! Overcome by delusion, I pressed aside my lord and father's command and came here after gathering this whole company. Good and evil, high and low, nectar and immortality, poison and death—the world has never seen or heard of anyone inwardly erasing Rāma's command. Yet I acted boldly in every way, and my Lord accepted it as a servant's loving service. By your own mercy and goodness, Lord, you made my evil good: my faults became like ornaments, and lovely fame spread in all four directions.’

words.grammar: epithet of Rāma; the selected source has the transposed nasal spelling अतंरजामी
words.sourceRef: selected repository witness; compare the recurrent form अंतरजामी elsewhere in the corpus

entries.meaning: ‘Your custom, gracious speech, and greatness are known throughout the world and sung by Veda and Āgama. Even those who are cruel, crooked, wicked, malicious, stained, base, unprincipled, destitute, and reckless are accepted if they hear of refuge, come before you, and bow just once. You never bring their faults into your heart; instead you hear their virtues proclaimed in saintly assemblies. What other master has honored a servant so and personally prepared the entire company and all its provisions? Even in a dream you do not consider your own deeds, but take a servant's embarrassment and grief into your own heart. There is no second Lord like that—raising my arm, I establish this vow. An animal dances and a parrot becomes skilled in recitation; their virtue and performance depend upon the trainer and teacher. By reforming and honoring people in this way you make them crest-jewels among saints. Who but the Compassionate One will forcibly uphold his renowned title as protector?’

‘Whether through grief and love or the nature of a child, I came here putting your command behind me. Even then, Merciful Lord, you looked only to your own gracious side and regarded everything I did as good. I beheld your feet, the root of every blessing, and knew my master to be naturally favorable. Before the great assembly I saw how fortunate I was: my great offense became my master's affection. The treasury of compassion fully satisfied every limb with grace and favor. My Lord preserved his indulgence toward me through the goodness of his own character and nature. Lord, I behaved with utter audacity, abandoning all reserve before my master and the assembly. Whether my speech is courteous or discourteous, please forgive it in whatever way you please, knowing my acute distress. To say too much to a benevolent, wise, gracious master is itself a grave fault. God, give your command now and set all my affairs right.’

‘I invoke the dust of my Lord's lotus feet, the lovely boundary of truth, merit, happiness, and welfare. By it I tell the desire of my own heart—the desire I have awake, asleep, and in dreams: naturally and lovingly to serve my master, abandoning self-interest, deception, reward, and the four aims of life. There is no service to a gracious master equal to obedience; may the Lord grant that favor to his servant.’ Saying this, Bharata was overcome by profound love; his body thrilled and his eyes filled with tears. In anguish he clasped the Lord's lotus feet; neither the moment nor that affection can be described. The ocean of compassion honored him with gracious words, took his hand, and seated him nearby. Hearing Bharata's plea and seeing his disposition, Raghurāya and the assembly grew limp with affection.

Indra is the extreme limit of deception and crookedness: another's ruin is dear to him as his own success. Like a crow, the foe of Pāka is deceitful and impure, and nowhere worthy of trust. First he gathered his evil design and deceit, then placed the resulting disquiet upon everyone's head. Divine illusion bewildered all the people, though it could not separate them from their immense love for Rāma. Under fear and restlessness their minds would not remain steady: one moment the forest appealed to them and the next their homes seemed pleasant. The suffering subjects' divided state of mind was like water at the meeting of river and sea. Double-minded, they found contentment nowhere, yet told one another nothing of the secret within. Seeing this, the treasury of compassion laughed inwardly and said that Maghavān's tongue was like a dog's. Leaving Bharata, Janaka, the sages, ministers, and attentive saints untouched, the divine illusion fastened upon everyone else according to the opening it found.

The ocean of compassion saw the people afflicted by their own affection and by the heavy deception of the lord of gods. King, guru, brahmins, ministers, and the assembly were all controlled by Bharata's devotion as if their minds were worked by a mechanism. They gazed toward Rāma like figures in a painting, and when they spoke timidly their words seemed rehearsed. Bharata's love, reverence, humility, and greatness give joy when heard but are difficult to describe. At the mere trace of his devotion, sages and the lord of Mithilā became immersed in love—how then can Tulasī tell Bharata's greatness? Through his natural devotion, good understanding blossomed in the poet's heart; yet knowing himself small and the subject great, he accepted the restraint of the poetic tradition and grew hesitant. Intellect cannot tell the abundance and charm of those virtues; its reach is like the speech of a child. Bharata's stainless fame is a spotless moon, and the poet's good understanding a young cakora bird, risen in the clear sky of a devotee's heart and gazing at it without a blink.

Bharata's nature is not easily reached even by the Vedas; forgive the fickleness of the poet's small intellect. Who can truthfully hear or tell Bharata's feeling and not become attached to Sītā and Rāma's feet? Whoever does not readily gain love for Rāma by remembering Bharata—who could be more ill-fated than that person? Seeing everyone's condition, the compassionate and wise Rāma knew what lay in each servant's heart. Pillar of duty, steadfast master of policy, ocean of truth, affection, character, and happiness, Raghurāja took account of country, time, occasion, and assembly. He spoke words that seemed the very wealth of speech: beneficial in outcome and, to the ear, like the moon's nectar. ‘Dear Bharata, you are a pillar of duty, versed in worldly and Vedic ways and accomplished in love. Your deeds, words, and thoughts are stainless and none is equal to you, dear child. How could your virtues be spoken in this adverse time, before the guru's assembly and your younger brother?’

‘Dear child, you know the custom of the Solar line and the truthful father's fame and love. You understand the occasion and assembly, the respect due to elders, and the mind's disinterest in its own benefit or harm. You know everyone's duty, and the supreme welfare and obligation of both you and me. I trust you in every way; nevertheless I speak as the occasion requires. Dear brother, without our father our entire affair has been sustained only through the grace of the guru's house. Otherwise subjects, relatives, family, and we ourselves would all have been ruined. If the sun appeared outside its proper time, tell me, whom in the world would it not distress? Destiny produced just such a calamity, dear child, but the sages and the lord of Mithilā have preserved everything. The kingdom's affairs, honor, householder's duty, earth, wealth, and home—all will be protected by the guru's power, and the outcome will be good for everyone.’
